recognitions.title: This week, three separate claims of having fixed something didn't survive a single news cycle
recognitions.explanation: Across trade, foreign policy and debt management, the same pattern showed up: an announcement of control or resolution, followed within about a day by the other side, or the market, contradicting it. This week one of the three went all the way - the Canada 'deal' didn't just fail to hold, it collapsed entirely into real tariffs and real retaliation. A denial that talks with Iran even exist, followed a day later by a declared war footing against that same government. A bond-market intervention whose relief lasted less than 24 hours before yields fully round-tripped. The pattern isn't that these claims are false when made - it's that none of them are built to survive contact with the next news cycle.

evidence.text: CENTCOM's own redirected-vessel count climbed from 86 to 92 in four days while the administration keeps framing the strait as being kept open - the US sank three Iranian tankers Saturday, Iran claims it hit three US-affiliated vessels back, and Iran's parliament speaker is warning of a "faster, heavier" response. "Managed" and "escalating" cannot both be the real word.

The 10-year has now reversed direction three times in five sessions: a Fed-comment-driven high above 4.81%, a dovish-remark dip to 4.74-4.77%, and a bounce back to 4.79% on a stronger-than-forecast August jobs report, pushing rate-hike odds back up to ~52%. No single reading has held for even a full trading day.

Trump called it the "biggest oil deal in history"; Chevron's own separate expansion - $7B aimed at doubling its Venezuela output to ~600,000 barrels a day - is the first evidence that actually stands independent of either government's telling, arriving as the underlying deal's legitimacy fight remains unresolved.

recognitions.title: Three things that looked like resolutions this week all deferred the real question to later
recognitions.explanation: A ceasefire, a court ruling, and a shipping framework all landed this week wearing the shape of a resolution — and in each case, the people closest to it said out loud that the actual question is still open. A peace roadmap got its first verification mission, not a verified peace. A Supreme Court stay resolved a procedural fight while its own justices noted the underlying legality is untouched. A transit deal is 'in principle' and 'still being finalized.' Each is a real step. None of them is the thing a headline would make it sound like.

evidence.text: The "negotiation track" produced a US strike on a wedding in Kuhestak on Sept 1 - 4-5 dead, dozens wounded, Iran vowing "a heavy cost." A shipping-corridor dispute that both sides still call diplomacy now has a civilian funeral attached to it.

A judge voided NY's $75B Climate Superfund Act, and coverage treated it as case-closed - but climate advocates are publicly pressing the state to appeal, calling the ruling "far from the last word," and the same court has already set a Sept 14 status-report deadline. The ruling resolved a hearing, not the question.

Putin and Pashinyan left their Bishkek meeting with incompatible accounts of what it settled - and now Kocharyan himself has broken his prison silence, warning "this must come to an end, or everyone should start learning Turkish." The detained man is making the same existential argument as the government that jailed him, just about the opposite outcome.

Judge Talwani spelled out exactly what the Supreme Court's win didn't do: she rejected the government's "cynical interpretation" of the ruling directly, writing the justices had "not endorsed the view that any challenge to the final rule is now too late." A procedural win got read by the government as a substantive one - a judge on record saying that reading is wrong.
